summary: Defines a new LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV for the PCEP LSP object. The original Flag field is only 12 bits, and all of them were already assigned, so this gives a place for more flags.

plainLanguage.summary: PCEP lets a controller ask a path computation element to set up network paths. The LSP object in that protocol has 12 flag bits, and every bit already has a meaning. This RFC adds a second, variable-length field of flags so that later specifications can add new ones without changing the protocol.

questions: what to do when pcep lsp flags are full
what is the pcep lsp-extended-flag tlv
why was the pcep lsp flag field extended
what is tlv type 64 in pcep
subtitle: A second, variable-length flag field for the PCEP LSP object, added after its 12 original flag bits were all taken.

tldr.problem: The LSP object in PCEP carries a Flag field of 12 bits, and every one of those bits already has a defined meaning, so there is no room left for new flags.
tldr.mechanism: A new TLV called LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG, type 64, carries an array of 32-bit flag units in the LSP object. This RFC defines the container only and assigns no flags to it.
tldr.outcome: Later documents can add LSP flags without inventing another TLV. Receivers ignore flags they do not understand, and a receiver that does not know the TLV ignores it entirely. RFC 9357 has since been updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 9357 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2023, and it has since been updated by RFC 9756. The document defines only the container for future flags: the bits stay unassigned until later documents assign them.

sections.title: Why the Flag Field Ran Out
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) runs between a Path Computation Element (PCE) and a Path Computation Client (PCC), or between two PCEs, so that paths for Multi-protocol Label Switching for Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) can be computed. RFC 5440 defines the protocol. RFC 8231 adds extensions for a stateful PCE, where the PCE keeps and updates state for the paths it manages.

One of those extensions is the LSP object, which carries a Flag field whose bits signal things such as delegation, synchronization and removal. As defined in RFC 8231, that field is 12 bits long, and Table 1 of this RFC shows that all 12 bits already have a meaning: PCE-allocation, ERO-compression, Fragmentation, P2MP, Create, a three-bit Operational value, Administrative, Remove, SYNC and Delegate.

Because every bit is taken, no new flag can be added to that field. This RFC leaves the original field alone and instead defines a separate TLV, the LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV, that carries an extended Flag field inside the same LSP object.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEP is the protocol a network controller uses to ask for paths. The LSP object it carries has 12 flag bits, and every one of them is already in use. This RFC adds a second field of flags so that new flags can be defined later.

sections.title: The LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV
sections.content:
The new TLV follows the format of every other PCEP TLV, as defined in RFC 5440. It carries a 16-bit Type field set to 64, a 16-bit Length field, and a value that holds the flags.

Length counts the bytes of the value. It MUST be a multiple of 4 and greater than 0. The value is an array of units of 32-bit flags, numbered from the most significant bit as bit zero, so each bit in a unit carries one LSP flag. A bit can stand for an operation, a feature or a state.

The field SHOULD use the minimum amount of space needed to encode the flag bits. This document assigns no bits at all. Unassigned bits MUST be set to zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt. As an example of intended use, the RFC notes that an E-flag for entropy label configuration was requested in a work in progress on the PCEP extension for the SR-MPLS entropy label position.
sections.plainLanguage: The new TLV carries a list of flag bits, 32 bits at a time. Its length must be a multiple of 4 bytes. This RFC reserves the space but assigns no flags to it.

sections.title: How Receivers Process the TLV
sections.content:
Flags are allocated starting from the most significant bit of each 32-bit unit. An implementation that does not support a particular flag MUST set that flag to zero when it transmits the object, and an implementation that does not understand a particular flag MUST ignore it. PCEP peers MUST handle TLVs of varying lengths.

When a speaker receives a TLV longer than it currently supports, it MUST ignore the bits beyond the length it understands. When it receives a TLV shorter than the one its implementation supports, it MUST act as if the bits beyond that length were not set.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender sets any flag it does not support to zero, and a receiver ignores any flag it does not understand. If the flag list is longer or shorter than the receiver expects, the receiver uses only the part it knows and treats the rest as unset.

sections.title: Advice for Defining New Flags
sections.content: Following the model given in Section 3.1 of RFC 8786, this RFC gives guidance for later documents that define additional flags. Each such document is expected to describe the interaction between the new flags and the existing ones. In particular, a new specification is expected to explain how to handle the case where both a new flag and a pre-existing flag are set. It is also expected to discuss any security implications of the additional flags and of their interaction with the existing flags.
sections.plainLanguage: A document that adds a new flag has to explain how that flag combines with the flags already in use, and what security effects it has.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
The RFC states that the LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV does not raise any backward compatibility issues. An implementation that does not understand or support the TLV MUST ignore it, as RFC 5440 requires for TLVs it does not recognise.

Any additional bits in the TLV that an implementation does not understand MUST be ignored. Future documents that define bits in the TLV are expected to define the error handling required for the case where the TLV is missing although it must be present.
sections.plainLanguage: Equipment that does not know the new TLV skips it, so older and newer implementations can talk to each other unchanged. Later documents that use the TLV must say what to do when it is missing.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA allocated the value 64 in the 'PCEP TLV Type Indicators' registry, which sits inside the 'Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP) Numbers' registry. The same body created a new registry, the 'LSP-EXTENDED-FLAG TLV Flag Field', to manage the bits of the new field. New values are assigned by Standards Action, as described in RFC 8126.

Each bit in the registry is tracked with three pieces of information: the bit number, counting from bit 0 as the most significant bit, a capability description, and a reference to the document that defines it. No values are currently defined. Bits 0 to 31 are initially marked 'Unassigned', and bits with a higher ordinal than 31 will be added to the registry in future documents if they are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps a public list of the flag bits in the new field. Each entry records the bit number, what the bit does, and the document that defines it. All 32 bits are unassigned so far.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content: An implementation that receives LSP Extended Flags it does not recognise MAY log them. The RFC suggests this because it helps diagnose backward compatibility problems with future features that make use of those flags.
sections.plainLanguage: An implementation may write a log entry when it sees a flag it does not recognise. That makes it easier to spot problems with a later feature.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 8231 sets out the security considerations for PCEP used with a stateful PCE, and this document does not change them. The security considerations for the LSP object flags are given in RFC 8231, RFC 8281, RFC 8623 and the work in progress on carrying the binding label and segment identifier in PCE-based networks.

Because the RFC opens the door to future flags, any document that specifies new flags must also discuss any associated security implications. No additional security issues are raised here beyond those in the referenced documents. RFC 8231 recommends that the stateful PCEP extension be authenticated and encrypted using Transport Layer Security (TLS), as set out in RFC 8253 and the current best practice in RFC 9325. When that recommendation is followed, the flags are protected by TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: This document adds no security rules of its own. The flags travel inside PCEP, and RFC 8231 says that PCEP with a stateful PCE should be authenticated and encrypted with TLS, so the flags are protected along with the rest of the session.
